prompt:
(a) State what is meant by a zero error. [1]
(b) Explain why a zero error is classified as a systematic error. [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: Part (a): A non-zero reading shown by an instrument when the true value of the quantity being measured is zero.
Part (b): It causes every subsequent measurement to be shifted by the same constant amount in the same direction.

hints: What should an instrument read when nothing is being measured?
How does this non-zero starting value affect later readings?
solution: (a) A zero error is a non-zero reading displayed by an instrument when the true input is zero. (b) It is a systematic error because it adds the same constant offset in the same direction to all measurements.
teacher_walkthrough: (a) Define zero error: when the input is zero (e.g. empty balance or closed calipers), the instrument displays a non-zero reading.
(b) Explain systematic nature: because that fixed initial offset is added to or subtracted from every reading, all measurements are shifted in the same direction.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored drill linking zero error directly to systematic error classification.
